issues.title: RI retirement income subtraction applies single cap to tax unit instead of per-person cap
issues.body:
## Summary

The Rhode Island retirement income subtraction incorrectly applies a single $20,000 cap to the combined pension income of both spouses, instead of a $20,000 cap per person. This results in joint filers receiving only $20,000 in subtraction instead of up to $40,000.

## Root Cause

In `/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ri/tax/income/agi/subtractions/taxable_retirement_income/ri_retirement_income_subtraction.py`:

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    person = tax_unit.members
    taxable_pension = person("taxable_pension_income", period)
    head_or_spouse = person("is_tax_unit_head_or_spouse", period)
    p = parameters(
        period
    ).gov.states.ri.tax.income.agi.subtractions.taxable_retirement_income
    total_taxable_pension = tax_unit.sum(taxable_pension * head_or_spouse)
    return min_(total_taxable_pension, p.cap)  # BUG: Single cap for entire tax unit
```

The code sums both spouses' pension income first, then applies a single $20,000 cap. But RI law applies the cap **per person**.

## Legal Reference

From the [Rhode Island Retirement Income Tax Guide](https://tax.ri.gov/sites/g/files/xkgbur541/files/2024-03/PUB_2024-01_retirement_income_guide.pdf):

> "This modification continues to be applied on an **individual basis**, meaning that **joint filers may qualify for a combined total of up to $40,000** (if both spouses qualify)."

RIGL § 44-30-12(c)(9) provides for the retirement income modification.

## Example (from policyengine-taxsim issue #670)

**Input:**
- MFJ, both age 75
- Person 1 pension: $42,767
- Person 2 pension: $42,767
- Total pension: $85,534
- Gross Social Security: $15,323

**PE calculates (wrong):**
- Pension subtraction: min($85,534, $20,000) = $20,000
- SS subtraction: $13,025
- Total subtractions: $33,025
- RI Modified AGI: $65,570
- RI Tax: $1,295

**TaxAct (correct):**
- Pension subtraction: min($42,767, $20,000) + min($42,767, $20,000) = $40,000
- SS subtraction: $13,024
- Total subtractions: $53,024
- RI Modified AGI: $45,569
- RI Tax: $545

## Files to Fix

`/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ri/tax/income/agi/subtractions/taxable_retirement_income/ri_retirement_income_subtraction.py`

## Suggested Fix

Change from:
```python
total_taxable_pension = tax_unit.sum(taxable_pension * head_or_spouse)
return min_(total_taxable_pension, p.cap)
```

To:
```python
capped_per_person = min_(taxable_pension, p.cap) * head_or_spouse
return tax_unit.sum(capped_per_person)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: RI retirement income subtraction applied per person for joint filers
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 75
        social_security_retirement: 7661.52
        taxable_private_pension_income: 42766.67
        taxable_interest_income: 18.58
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 75
        social_security_retirement: 7661.52
        taxable_private_pension_income: 42766.67
        taxable_interest_income: 18.58
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 44
  output:
    ri_retirement_income_subtraction: 40000  # $20K per person, not $20K total
    ri_agi: 45569
    ri_income_tax: 545
```

## Related Issues

- PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim#670: RI joint 2024 elderly 85Kpensions 15Kgssi

issues.title: CT Social Security benefit adjustment uses 85% of gross SS instead of actual federal taxable SS
issues.body:
## Summary

The CT Social Security benefit adjustment incorrectly uses `gross_ss * 0.85` for Line E of the worksheet, but should use the actual federal taxable Social Security amount (`tax_unit_taxable_social_security`).

## Root Cause

In `/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ct/tax/income/subtractions/ct_social_security_benefit_adjustment.py`, lines 37-40:

```python
# Part E (Line 18 from federal social security worksheet)
gross_ss = tax_unit("tax_unit_social_security", period)
adjusted_gross_social_security = (
    gross_ss * p_irs.rate.additional.excess  # BUG: Always uses 85% of gross
)
```

The CT worksheet instructions state Line E should be:
> "Taxable amount of Social Security benefits reported on your 2024 federal Social Security Benefits Worksheet, Line 18"

This is the **actual federal taxable SS amount**, not simply 85% of gross SS. The 85% is a maximum cap, but the actual taxable amount can be lower depending on combined income.

## Legal Reference

[CT-1040 Instructions, Social Security Benefit Adjustment Worksheet](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/DRS/Forms/2024/Income/CT-1040-Instructions_1224.pdf):

> **Line E**: Taxable amount of Social Security benefits reported on your 2024 federal Social Security Benefits Worksheet, Line 18

## Example (from policyengine-taxsim issue #671)

**Input:**
- MFJ, both age 75
- Gross Social Security: $93,438
- Taxable pensions: $56,950
- Federal AGI: $113,669
- Federal Taxable SS: $56,719

**PE calculates (wrong):**
- Line E: $93,438 × 0.85 = $79,422
- CT SS Adjustment: $79,422 - $17,917 = $61,505
- CT AGI: $113,669 - $61,505 - $31,323 = $20,841
- CT Tax: $0

**TaxAct (correct):**
- Line E: $56,719 (actual federal taxable SS)
- CT SS Adjustment: $56,719 - $17,917 = $38,802
- CT AGI: $113,669 - $38,802 - $31,323 = $43,544
- CT Tax: $332

## Files to Fix

`/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ct/tax/income/subtractions/ct_social_security_benefit_adjustment.py`

## Suggested Fix

Change lines 37-40 from:
```python
# Part E (Line 18 from federal social security worksheet)
gross_ss = tax_unit("tax_unit_social_security", period)
adjusted_gross_social_security = (
    gross_ss * p_irs.rate.additional.excess
)
```

To:
```python
# Part E (Line 18 from federal social security worksheet)
adjusted_gross_social_security = tax_unit(
    "tax_unit_taxable_social_security", period
)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: CT Social Security adjustment uses actual federal taxable SS
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 75
        social_security_retirement: 46718.91
        taxable_private_pension_income: 28475.02
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 75
        social_security_retirement: 46718.91
        taxable_private_pension_income: 28475.02
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 9
  output:
    ct_social_security_benefit_adjustment: 38802  # Not 61505
    ct_agi: 43544  # Not 20841
    ct_income_tax: 332  # Not 0
```

issues.title: NY supplemental tax broken for ultra-high income; Worksheet 11 not applied correctly
issues.body:
## Summary

PolicyEngine's NY supplemental tax calculation fails for ultra-high income taxpayers (NY AGI > $25,000,000) because the code uses `thresholds[-1]` which returns `inf` for 2024, causing the Worksheet 11 flat 10.9% rate to never be applied.

## Root Cause

In `/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ny/tax/income/ny_supplemental_tax.py`:

```python
agi_limit = select(
    in_each_status,
    [
        single.thresholds[-1],  # Returns inf for 2024!
        joint.thresholds[-1],
        ...
    ],
)
# ...
return where(
    ny_agi > agi_limit,  # Always False because nothing > infinity!
    supplemental_tax_high_agi,  # Correct Worksheet 11 calculation
    supplemental_tax_general,   # Wrong path taken
)
```

For 2024, the NY single rate schedule thresholds are:
```
[0, 8500, 11700, 13900, 80650, 215400, 1077550, 5000000, 25000000, inf]
```

Since `thresholds[-1]` = `inf`, the condition `ny_agi > agi_limit` is always False, so PE uses `supplemental_tax_general` instead of `supplemental_tax_high_agi`.

## Legal Reference

[NY Tax Computation Worksheet 11](https://www.tax.ny.gov/pdf/2024/inc/it201i_2024.pdf):

> "If your New York AGI is more than $25,000,000, then you must compute your tax using this worksheet."
>
> Tax = Taxable Income × 10.9%

This is a **flat 10.9% rate on ALL taxable income**, not the graduated rate schedule.

## Example (from policyengine-taxsim issue #672)

**Input:**
- Single, age 75
- Wages: $109,246,904
- Pensions: $50,270
- Interest: $1,538,933
- NY AGI: $110,816,112

**PE calculates:**
- NY Main Tax (graduated): $11,863,014
- NY Supplemental Tax: $65,071
- Total: **$11,928,085**

**TaxAct (correct) using Worksheet 11:**
- Tax = $110,808,106 × 10.9% = **$12,078,084**

**Difference: $149,999** (~$150K undertaxed)

## Files to Fix

`/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ny/tax/income/ny_supplemental_tax.py`

## Suggested Fix

Option 1: Use `thresholds[-2]` to get the $25M threshold:
```python
agi_limit = select(
    in_each_status,
    [
        single.thresholds[-2],  # $25,000,000 for 2024
        ...
    ],
)
```

Option 2: Add explicit parameter for Worksheet 11 threshold:
```python
worksheet_11_threshold = p.worksheet_11_agi_threshold  # New parameter = $25M
return where(
    ny_agi > worksheet_11_threshold,
    ny_taxable_income * 0.109,  # Flat Worksheet 11 rate
    supplemental_tax_general + ny_main_income_tax,
)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: NY Worksheet 11 - ultra-high income flat 10.9% rate
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 10
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 75
        employment_income: 109246904
        taxable_private_pension_income: 50270.32
        taxable_interest_income: 1538932.8
        is_tax_unit_head: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1]
        state_fips: 36
  output:
    ny_income_tax: 12078084  # Worksheet 11: taxable_income * 10.9%
```

## Related Issues

- policyengine-taxsim#672: NY single elderly 109246Kpwages 50Kpensions 1538intrec

issues.title: NJ gross income incorrectly includes net losses from income categories; missing 'same category rule'
issues.body:
## Summary

PolicyEngine's New Jersey gross income calculation incorrectly includes net losses from income categories like capital gains and S-corp income. Under NJ's unique "same category rule" (N.J.S. 54A:5-1), if any of the 16 income categories has a net loss, that loss must be **disregarded** (treated as $0) - it cannot offset income from other categories.

## Root Cause

In `/policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/nj/tax/income/adjusted_gross_income/nj_gross_income.py`:

```python
class nj_gross_income(Variable):
    adds = "gov.states.nj.tax.income.gross_income_sources"
```

The `gross_income_sources.yaml` includes:
- `long_term_capital_gains`
- `short_term_capital_gains`
- `partnership_s_corp_income`

These are added directly without applying NJ's rule that net losses in any category must be disregarded.

## Legal Reference

**N.J.S. 54A:5-1** defines 16 separate categories of gross income:
- Category (a): Salaries, wages, tips
- Category (c): Net gains from disposition of property (capital gains)
- Category (e): Interest
- Category (f): Dividends
- Category (k): Distributive share of partnership income
- Category (p): Net pro rata share of S corporation income
- etc.

**The "Same Category Rule"**: Losses within one category can offset gains in that same category, but a **net loss in any category is disregarded** when computing total NJ gross income. Losses cannot:
- Offset income from other categories
- Be carried forward to future years

From the [NJ Division of Taxation](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/njit9.shtml):
> "You can deduct federal passive losses in full in the year incurred against any gain within the **same category** of income"

## Example (from policyengine-taxsim issue #673)

**Input:**
- MFJ, ages 54 and 54
- Wages: $136,639
- Interest: $343
- Dividends: $1,661
- Short-term capital losses: -$237,873
- Long-term capital losses: -$2,252
- S-corp losses: -$29,134

**PE calculates:**
- NJ Gross Income: **-$133,628** (incorrectly includes full losses)
- NJ AGI: $3,011
- NJ Tax: $0

**TaxAct (correct) calculates:**
- NJ Gross Income: **$138,673** (losses disregarded per same category rule)
  - Wages: $136,639
  - Interest: $343
  - Dividends: $1,661
  - Capital gains: $0 (net loss → disregarded)
  - S-corp: $0 (net loss → disregarded)
  - Other: $30
- NJ Tax: **$4,776**

## Files to Fix

1. **`policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/nj/tax/income/adjusted_gross_income/nj_gross_income.py`**
   - Restructure to calculate each NJ income category separately
   - Apply `max_(0, category_total)` to each category before summing

2. **New variables needed** for NJ income categories:
   - `nj_category_c_income` (capital gains - net of losses, capped at 0)
   - `nj_category_k_income` (partnership income - net, capped at 0)
   - `nj_category_p_income` (S-corp income - net, capped at 0)
   - etc.

## Suggested Fix

```python
class nj_gross_income(Variable):
    value_type = float
    entity = Person
    label = "New Jersey gross income"
    unit = USD
    definition_period = YEAR
    defined_for = StateCode.NJ

    def formula(person, period, parameters):
        # Category (a): Wages - always positive
        cat_a = person("employment_income", period)
        
        # Category (c): Net gains from disposition of property
        # Net loss is disregarded (capped at 0)
        cat_c = max_(0, 
            person("short_term_capital_gains", period) +
            person("long_term_capital_gains", period)
        )
        
        # Category (e): Interest
        cat_e = person("taxable_interest_income", period)
        
        # Category (f): Dividends
        cat_f = person("dividend_income", period)
        
        # Category (k): Partnership income - net loss disregarded
        # Category (p): S-corp income - net loss disregarded
        cat_k_p = max_(0, person("partnership_s_corp_income", period))
        
        # ... other categories ...
        
        # Sum all categories (each already capped at 0 if net loss)
        return cat_a + cat_c + cat_e + cat_f + cat_k_p + ...
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: NJ same category rule - capital and S-corp losses disregarded
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 54
        employment_income: 0
        qualified_dividend_income: 830.69
        long_term_capital_gains: -1126.16
        short_term_capital_gains: -118936.69
        partnership_s_corp_income: -14566.96
        taxable_interest_income: 171.53
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 54
        employment_income: 136639.06
        qualified_dividend_income: 830.69
        long_term_capital_gains: -1126.16
        short_term_capital_gains: -118936.69
        partnership_s_corp_income: -14566.96
        taxable_interest_income: 171.53
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 34
  output:
    nj_gross_income: 138673  # Losses disregarded per same category rule
    nj_income_tax: 4776
```

issues.title: Partnership/S-corp losses not included in AGI; missing Section 461(l) excess business loss limitation
issues.body:
## Summary

PolicyEngine does not include partnership/S-corp losses in adjusted gross income. The `irs_gross_income` variable caps all income sources at 0 (line 19: `max_(0, ...)`), and `loss_ald` only handles self-employment and capital losses—not partnership/S-corp losses. Additionally, the Section 461(l) excess business loss limitation is not implemented.

## Root Cause

### 1. S-corp losses ignored in gross income

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/irs/income/taxable_income/adjusted_gross_income/irs_gross_income/irs_gross_income.py`:

```python
def formula(person, period, parameters):
    sources = parameters(period).gov.irs.gross_income.sources
    total = 0
    not_dependent = ~person("is_tax_unit_dependent", period)
    for source in sources:
        # Add positive values only - losses are deducted later.
        total += not_dependent * max_(0, add(person, period, [source]))  # <-- caps at 0
    return total
```

### 2. S-corp losses not deducted in loss_ald

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/irs/income/taxable_income/adjusted_gross_income/above_the_line_deductions/loss_ald.py`:

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    # Only handles self_employment_income - NOT partnership_s_corp_income
    indiv_se_loss = max_(0, -person("self_employment_income", period))
    self_employment_loss = tax_unit.sum(indiv_se_loss)
    limited_capital_loss = tax_unit("limited_capital_loss", period)
    return min_(max_loss, self_employment_loss + limited_capital_loss)
```

### 3. Section 461(l) not implemented

IRC §461(l) limits excess business losses for noncorporate taxpayers. For 2024:
- **Single/Other**: $305,000
- **MFJ**: $610,000

Losses exceeding this threshold become NOL carryforwards.

## Legal Reference

[26 U.S.C. §461(l)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/461):

> **(1) Limitation** — In the case of a taxpayer other than a corporation, any excess business loss of the taxpayer for the taxable year shall not be allowed.
>
> **(3) Excess business loss** — The term "excess business loss" means the excess (if any) of—
> - (i) the aggregate deductions attributable to trades or businesses... over
> - (ii) the sum of aggregate gross income/gain from trades or businesses, plus $250,000 ($500,000 MFJ, indexed for inflation)

## Example (from policyengine-taxsim issue #674)

**Input:**
- MFJ, ages 26 and 27
- Spouse wages: $82,813
- S-corp loss: -$838,974
- Capital losses: -$224,839
- Interest: $20

**PE calculates:**
- Federal AGI: $79,833 (S-corp loss completely ignored)
- Only $3,000 capital loss deducted

**TaxAct (correct) calculates:**
- S-corp loss on Schedule E: -$838,974
- Form 461 limitation: $610,000 threshold
- Excess business loss add-back: +$228,974
- Federal AGI: **-$530,137**

## Files to Fix

1. `policyengine_us/variables/gov/irs/income/taxable_income/adjusted_gross_income/above_the_line_deductions/loss_ald.py`
   - Add `partnership_s_corp_income` losses to the deduction

2. New file needed for Section 461(l):
   - `policyengine_us/variables/gov/irs/income/taxable_income/adjusted_gross_income/excess_business_loss_limitation.py`
   - Implement Form 461 calculation

3. New parameters needed:
   - `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/irs/ald/loss/excess_business_loss_threshold.yaml`
   - 2024: $305,000 (single) / $610,000 (MFJ)

## Suggested Fix

### Step 1: Add S-corp losses to loss_ald.py

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    filing_status = tax_unit("filing_status", period)
    max_loss = parameters(period).gov.irs.ald.loss.max[filing_status]
    person = tax_unit.members
    
    # Self-employment losses
    indiv_se_loss = max_(0, -person("self_employment_income", period))
    self_employment_loss = tax_unit.sum(indiv_se_loss)
    
    # Partnership/S-corp losses (NEW)
    indiv_scorp_loss = max_(0, -person("partnership_s_corp_income", period))
    partnership_s_corp_loss = tax_unit.sum(indiv_scorp_loss)
    
    # Capital losses
    limited_capital_loss = tax_unit("limited_capital_loss", period)
    
    # Apply Section 461(l) limitation to business losses
    total_business_loss = self_employment_loss + partnership_s_corp_loss
    excess_business_loss_threshold = parameters(period).gov.irs.ald.loss.excess_business_loss_threshold[filing_status]
    limited_business_loss = min_(total_business_loss, excess_business_loss_threshold)
    
    return min_(max_loss, limited_business_loss + limited_capital_loss)
```

### Step 2: Add threshold parameter

```yaml
# excess_business_loss_threshold.yaml
description: Section 461(l) excess business loss threshold for noncorporate taxpayers.
metadata:
  reference:
    - title: 26 U.S.C. §461(l)(3)(A)(ii)(II)
      href: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/461
    - title: Form 461 Instructions
      href: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i461.pdf
  unit: currency-USD
  period: year
  label: Excess business loss threshold
SINGLE:
  2021-01-01: 262000
  2022-01-01: 270000
  2023-01-01: 289000
  2024-01-01: 305000
JOINT:
  2021-01-01: 524000
  2022-01-01: 540000
  2023-01-01: 578000
  2024-01-01: 610000
# Other filing statuses use single amount
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: S-corp loss with Section 461(l) limitation
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 26
        partnership_s_corp_income: -419487
        short_term_capital_gains: -111233
        long_term_capital_gains: -1187
        taxable_interest_income: 10
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 27
        employment_income: 82813
        partnership_s_corp_income: -419487
        short_term_capital_gains: -111233
        long_term_capital_gains: -1187
        taxable_interest_income: 10
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 44
  output:
    adjusted_gross_income: -530137  # Negative AGI after 461(l) limitation
```

## Related Issues

- PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim#674: RI joint 82Kpwages -838K psemp

issues.title: Fix trust fund revenue allocation: tob_revenue_oasdi and tob_revenue_medicare_hi use wrong split formula
issues.body:
## Summary

The `tob_revenue_oasdi` and `tob_revenue_medicare_hi` variables were using IRC §86 tier proportions for trust fund allocation, which does not follow the statutory requirements.

## Statutory Requirement

Per 42 U.S.C. 401 note (Section 121(e) of PL 98-21, as amended by OBRA 1993):
- **OASDI** receives tax revenue attributable to the "first 50%" of gross SS benefits
- **Medicare HI** receives tax revenue from the 1993 amendments (the 50%→85% increase)

## Correct Implementation: Double-Branching

The trust fund allocation must use **branching** to calculate marginal tax impact:

```
Scenario A: Tax with NO taxable SS (neutralized)
Scenario B: Tax with min(taxable_ss, 0.5 × gross_ss)
Scenario C: Tax with full taxable SS (current law)

OASDI revenue = B - A
HI revenue = C - B
```

This approach correctly captures the marginal tax rates:
- The "first 50%" (OASDI) is taxed at lower marginal rates since it is added first
- The additional 35% (HI) is stacked on top at higher marginal rates

## Why Tier-Based Allocation Was Wrong

The old tier-based approach used IRC §86 tier proportions, which include bracket caps ($4,500 single / $6,000 joint) that are unrelated to trust fund allocation rules.

## References

1. **PL 98-21 Section 121(e)(1)** - Original trust fund appropriations (1984)
2. **OBRA 1993 Section 13215(c)** - Medicare HI allocation amendment
3. **IRC §86** - Taxation of Social Security benefits (defines taxable amount, not allocation)

## Solution

Added parameter `gov.ssa.revenue.oasdi_share_of_gross_ss` (0.5) and implemented double-branching in both `tob_revenue_oasdi.py` and `tob_revenue_medicare_hi.py`.

issues.title: Head of Household should allow qualifying relatives (e.g., 19-year-old non-student dependents)
issues.body:
## Summary

PolicyEngine may incorrectly deny Head of Household (HOH) filing status when the qualifying person is a **qualifying relative** rather than a **qualifying child**. Specifically, a 19-year-old non-student child who is claimed as a dependent can qualify the parent for HOH status, even though they fail the qualifying child age test.

## Legal Basis

**IRC §2(b)(1)(A)** provides two pathways to HOH status:

> (A) maintains as his home a household which constitutes for more than one-half of such taxable year the principal place of abode, as a member of such household, of—
> 
> **(i)** a qualifying child of the individual (as defined in section 152(c)), ... **or**
> 
> **(ii) any other person who is a dependent of the taxpayer**, if the taxpayer is entitled to a deduction for the taxable year for such person under section 151

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2#b_1_A

### Two Types of Dependents

**IRC §152(a)** defines dependent as either:
1. A **qualifying child** - §152(c)
2. A **qualifying relative** - §152(d)

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/152#a

### Qualifying Child Age Test - §152(c)(3)(A)

> has not attained the age of 19 as of the close of the calendar year... or is a student who has not attained the age of 24...

A 19-year-old non-student **fails** this test and cannot be a qualifying child.

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/152#c_3_A

### Qualifying Relative - §152(d)(1)

Requirements:
- (A) Not a qualifying child of any taxpayer
- (B) Gross income < exemption amount (~$5,050 for 2024)
- (C) Taxpayer provides >50% of support
- (D) Meets relationship test

**No age test applies to qualifying relatives.**

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/152#d_1

### Exemption Amount During TCJA

Although TCJA suspended the personal exemption deduction (set to $0) for 2018-2025, the exemption **amount** is still calculated and used for the qualifying relative gross income test. For 2024, it's $5,050.

Source: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-23-34.pdf (page 4)

## Expected Behavior

| Scenario | Qualifying Child? | Qualifying Relative? | HOH Valid? |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------|------------|
| 19-yr-old, non-student, gross income < $5,050 | ❌ (fails age) | ✅ | ✅ via §2(b)(1)(A)(ii) |
| 19-yr-old, non-student, gross income ≥ $5,050 | ❌ (fails age) | ❌ (fails income) | ❌ Not a dependent |
| 19-yr-old, permanently disabled | ✅ (age waived) | N/A | ✅ via §2(b)(1)(A)(i) |

## Current Behavior

PolicyEngine may only check the qualifying child pathway (i) for HOH eligibility, not the qualifying relative pathway (ii).

## Files to Investigate

- Head of Household eligibility logic
- Qualifying relative determination
- Interaction between dependent status and filing status

## Related

- TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/652

issues.title: MA Part A AGI may double-count capital losses when LTCG >= STCG loss
issues.body:
## Summary

Massachusetts Part A AGI calculation may double-count short-term capital losses when:
1. Short-term capital losses exist
2. Positive long-term capital gains exist (≥ STCG loss amount)
3. Interest and/or dividends exist

This was discovered during review of PR #6969 (which correctly fixes Part C).

## Root Cause

In `ma_part_a_agi.py`, the calculation uses the **full** STCG loss amount against interest/dividends without considering how much was already "consumed" by offsetting LTCG in Part C.

```python
short_term_capital_loss = max_(0, -short_term_capital_gains)
# ...
short_term_loss_against_interest_dividends = min_(
    interest_dividends_deduction_cap,  # $2,000
    min_(
        interest_and_dividends,
        short_term_capital_loss,  # Uses FULL loss, not remaining after Part C
    ),
)
```

## Example Scenario

**Inputs:**
- Short-term capital gains: -$10,000 (loss)
- Long-term capital gains: +$10,000 (gain)
- Dividends: $5,000

**Per MA TIR 02-21 rules (correct behavior):**
1. STCG loss offsets LTCG: $10,000 vs $10,000 → $0 remaining loss
2. Remaining loss offsets dividends: $0 → $5,000 dividends remain taxable

**Current code behavior:**
- Part C: $10,000 LTCG - $10,000 loss = $0 ✅
- Part A: $5,000 dividends - $2,000 (from $10,000 loss, capped) = $3,000 ❌

**Result:** $12,000 of deductions claimed from $10,000 of losses

## Suggested Fix

Part A should calculate the remaining STCG loss after Part C consumption:

```python
# STCG losses used in Part C to offset LTCG
stcg_loss_used_in_part_c = min_(short_term_capital_loss, max_(0, long_term_capital_gains))
remaining_short_term_loss = short_term_capital_loss - stcg_loss_used_in_part_c

# Then use remaining_short_term_loss instead of short_term_capital_loss
short_term_loss_against_interest_dividends = min_(
    interest_dividends_deduction_cap,
    min_(
        interest_and_dividends,
        remaining_short_term_loss,  # Only use what's left after Part C
    ),
)
```

## Test Case

```yaml
- name: STCG loss fully consumed by LTCG should not offset dividends
  period: 2024
  input:
    short_term_capital_gains: -10_000
    long_term_capital_gains: 10_000
    dividend_income: 5_000
    state_code: MA
  output:
    ma_part_c_gross_income: 0  # LTCG offset by STCG loss
    ma_part_a_agi: 5_000  # Full dividends taxable (no remaining loss)
```

## References

- [MA TIR 02-21](https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-02-21-capital-gains-and-losses-massachusetts-tax-law-changes) - Loss offset hierarchy
- [MA Schedule B Instructions](https://www.mass.gov/doc/2024-schedule-b-interest-dividends-and-certain-capital-gains-and-losses/download)
- Related PR: #6969

## Files to Fix

issues.title: AZ Property Tax Credit incorrectly subtracts exemptions from household income
issues.body:
## Summary

The Arizona Property Tax Credit (Form 140-PTC) incorrectly calculates household income by using `az_agi`, which subtracts AZ exemptions. Form 140-PTC household income should be **gross income without exemptions**.

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/az/tax/income/credits/property_tax/income_sources.yaml`:

```yaml
values:
  2021-01-01:
    - capital_gains_excluded_from_taxable_income
    - tax_exempt_interest_income
    - public_pension_income
    - az_agi  # BUG: az_agi subtracts exemptions
```

The variable `az_agi` is calculated as:
```python
return max_(0, adjusted_gross_income + additions - subtractions - exemptions)
```

But Form 140-PTC Part 1 "Schedule of Household Income" lists **gross** income sources (wages, interest, dividends, etc.) with NO exemptions deducted.

## Example

Test case: AZ joint 2024, ages 81/73, $5,280 interest income, $17,139 rent

| Calculation | PE Value | Correct Value |
|-------------|----------|---------------|
| AZ exemptions | $4,200 | N/A for Form 140-PTC |
| Household income | $1,080 (`az_agi` after exemptions) | **$5,280** (gross) |
| Credit (Schedule 2) | $502 (for $0-$2,500 income) | **$78** (for $5,201-$5,350) |
| AZ income tax | -$552 | **~-$50** |

## Legal Basis

Form 140-PTC Part 1 "Schedule of Household Income" shows:
- Line A: Salaries, wages, tips
- Line B: **Dividend and interest income received** (gross)
- Line C: Business and farm income
- Line D: Gain or loss from sale of property
- Line E: Pension and annuity income
- etc.

**No exemptions are deducted** - this is gross household income.

Reference: https://azdor.gov/forms/tax-credits-forms/property-tax-refund-credit-claim-form-fillable

## Files to Fix

- `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/az/tax/income/credits/property_tax/income_sources.yaml`

## Suggested Fix

Replace `az_agi` with `adjusted_gross_income` (federal AGI) since federal AGI is gross income without AZ-specific exemptions:

```yaml
values:
  2021-01-01:
    - capital_gains_excluded_from_taxable_income
    - tax_exempt_interest_income
    - public_pension_income
    - adjusted_gross_income  # Federal AGI without AZ exemptions
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: AZ property tax credit uses gross household income without exemptions
  absolute_error_margin: 2
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 81
        taxable_interest_income: 2640.18
        rent: 17139.24
      person2:
        age: 73
        taxable_interest_income: 2640.18
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 4
  output:
    az_property_tax_credit: 78  # Schedule 2: $5,201-$5,350 income = $78 credit
```

## Related

- TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/473
- Previously closed PR #6498 only partially addressed this (changed interest source but didn't fix the exemption issue)

issues.title: ME Dependent Exemption Credit excludes Credit for Other Dependents (ODC) qualifying dependents
issues.body:
## Summary

The Maine Dependent Exemption Credit incorrectly excludes dependents who qualify for the federal Credit for Other Dependents (ODC). The current implementation only allows dependents who qualify for the federal Child Tax Credit (under age 17), but Maine law includes any dependent eligible under IRC Section 24, which includes the ODC for dependents age 17+.

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/me/tax/income/credits/dependent_exemption/me_dependent_exemption_credit_amount_person.py` line 11:

```python
defined_for = "ctc_qualifying_child"  # Only includes children under 17
```

This excludes dependents age 17+ who qualify for the federal Credit for Other Dependents under IRC §24(h)(4).

## Legal Basis

**Maine Statute 36 M.R.S. §5219-SS:**
> Taxpayers qualify if they "were eligible to claim the federal child tax credit **pursuant to the Code, Section 24**"

**IRC Section 24(h)(4) - Credit for Other Dependents:**
> "The credit determined under subsection (a)... shall be increased by $500 for each dependent of the taxpayer... who is not a qualifying child"

The ODC is explicitly part of Section 24, so dependents qualifying for ODC satisfy Maine's eligibility requirement.

**ME Form 1040ME Instructions (Line 13a):**
> "Enter the number of qualifying children and dependents for whom you are eligible to claim the **federal child tax credit or the credit for other dependents**"

Reference: https://www.mainelegislature.org/legis/statutes/36/title36sec5219-SS.html

## Files to Fix

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/me/tax/income/credits/dependent_exemption/me_dependent_exemption_credit_amount_person.py`

## Suggested Fix

Change line 11 from:
```python
defined_for = "ctc_qualifying_child"
```

To:
```python
defined_for = "is_tax_unit_dependent"
```

This includes all tax unit dependents, who by definition qualify for either the CTC (under 17) or the ODC (17+) under IRC Section 24.

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: ME dependent exemption credit includes ODC-qualifying dependent age 17
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      head:
        age: 70
        qualified_dividend_income: 8980.64
        taxable_interest_income: 1950.19
        long_term_capital_gains: 8149.55
        pension_income: 86460.30
      dependent:
        age: 17
        is_tax_unit_dependent: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [head, dependent]
        filing_status: HEAD_OF_HOUSEHOLD
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [head, dependent]
    households:
      household:
        members: [head, dependent]
        state_fips: 23  # Maine
  output:
    me_dependent_exemption_credit: 300  # $300 for 1 qualifying dependent
```

## Source

TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/568

issues.title: MN CTC should check investment income eligibility (same as WFC)
issues.body:
## Summary

Minnesota's Child Tax Credit (CTC) under §290.0661 requires the taxpayer to be "eligible for the credit under section 290.0671" (the Working Family Credit). This includes the investment income test. Currently, PE correctly disqualifies the WFC for high investment income, but incorrectly still allows the CTC.

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/mn/tax/income/credits/mn_child_and_working_families_credits_ctc_eligible_child.py`, the eligibility only checks:
1. Age < limit
2. EITC identification requirements (SSN)

It does NOT check whether the **taxpayer** passes the investment income test required by §290.0671.

## Legal Basis

[MN Statute §290.0661](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0661) states:

> "a taxpayer must be **eligible for the credit under section 290.0671**"

The only exception is for taxpayers with "insufficient earned income" - NOT for investment income disqualification.

[MN Statute §290.0671](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0671) requires eligibility under IRC §32, which includes the investment income limit ($11,600 for 2024).

## Test Case (from policyengine-taxsim #594)

- **Filing Status**: Married Filing Jointly
- **Year**: 2024
- **Wages**: $30,000
- **Interest Income**: $19,830 (exceeds $11,600 limit)
- **Dependents**: 1 child age 2

### Current PE Behavior

| Component | PE Value | Expected |
|-----------|----------|----------|
| WFC | $0 ✓ | $0 |
| CTC | $196 ✗ | $0 |
| Total | $196 ✗ | $0 |

TaxAct shows **0 qualifying children** and **$0** credit.

## Files to Fix

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/mn/tax/income/credits/mn_child_and_working_families_credits_ctc_eligible_child.py`
- Or modify `mn_child_and_working_families_credits.py` to check taxpayer eligibility before applying CTC

## Suggested Fix

Option 1: Add investment income check to CTC child eligibility (at person level, checking tax_unit):
```python
def formula(person, period, parameters):
    age = person("age", period)
    meets_eitc_identification_requirements = person(
        "meets_eitc_identification_requirements", period
    )
    p = parameters(period).gov.states.mn.tax.income.credits.cwfc.ctc
    age_eligible = age < p.age_limit
    # Add: Check taxpayer investment income eligibility
    invinc_eligible = person.tax_unit("eitc_investment_income_eligible", period)
    return age_eligible & meets_eitc_identification_requirements & invinc_eligible
```

Option 2: Modify the combined credit calculation to zero out CTC when taxpayer is investment income ineligible.

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: MN CTC disqualified by investment income
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 40
        employment_income: 30_000
        taxable_interest_income: 19_830
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 40
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
      child1:
        age: 2
        is_tax_unit_dependent: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
        state_fips: 27  # Minnesota
  output:
    eitc_investment_income_eligible: false
    mn_wfc: 0
    mn_child_and_working_families_credits: 0  # CTC should also be $0
```

## References

- [MN Statute §290.0661 (CTC)](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0661)
- [MN Statute §290.0671 (WFC)](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0671)
- [Form M1CWFC Instructions](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2024-01/m1cwfc-23_1.pdf)
- [policyengine-taxsim Issue #594](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/594)

issues.title: MD CDCC uses wrong federal credit variable (cdcc_potential instead of cdcc)
issues.body:
## Summary

Maryland's Child and Dependent Care Credit (CDCC) incorrectly uses the **potential** federal credit (`cdcc_potential` - Form 2441 Line 9c) instead of the **actual** federal credit (`cdcc` - Form 2441 Line 11, after the Credit Limitation Worksheet).

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/md/tax/income/credits/cdcc/md_cdcc.py` line 22:

```python
max_cdcc = p.percent * tax_unit("cdcc_potential", period)  # WRONG - Line 9c
```

Should be:

```python
max_cdcc = p.percent * tax_unit("cdcc", period)  # CORRECT - Line 11
```

## Legal Basis

[Maryland Tax-General § 10-716](https://law.justia.com/codes/maryland/tax-general/title-10/subtitle-7/section-10-716/) defines:

> **"Federal child and dependent care credit"** means the child and dependent care credit **properly claimed** by an individual for the taxable year under § 21 of the Internal Revenue Code.

The phrase "properly claimed" refers to the actual credit on the federal return (Form 2441 Line 11), not the potential credit before the tax liability limitation (Line 9c).

## Test Case (from policyengine-taxsim #608)

- **Filing Status**: Married Filing Jointly
- **Year**: 2024
- **Income**: $10K pwages + $10K swages + $101K dividends = $121K AGI
- **Child care expenses**: $6,000
- **Dependents**: 1 (age 10)

### Expected Calculation

1. Federal tax ≈ $0 (most income is qualified dividends at 0% capital gains rate)
2. Federal CDCC tax liability limit (Line 10) ≈ $0
3. Federal CDCC (Line 11) = min(potential, limit) = **$0**
4. MD CDCC = 32% × $0 = **$0**

### Current PE Behavior

PE uses `cdcc_potential` (Line 9c), which is non-zero (~$1,200), so MD CDCC incorrectly equals ~$384.

## Files to Fix

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/md/tax/income/credits/cdcc/md_cdcc.py`

## Suggested Fix

```python
# Line 22: Change from cdcc_potential to cdcc
max_cdcc = p.percent * tax_unit("cdcc", period)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: MD CDCC uses actual federal credit not potential
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 40
        employment_income: 10_000
        qualified_dividend_income: 50_500
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 40
        employment_income: 10_000
        qualified_dividend_income: 50_500
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
      child1:
        age: 10
        is_tax_unit_dependent: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
        tax_unit_childcare_expenses: 6_000
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2, child1]
        state_fips: 24  # Maryland
  output:
    md_cdcc: 0  # Federal CDCC is $0 due to tax liability limit, so MD CDCC is $0
```

## References

- [MD Tax-General § 10-716](https://law.justia.com/codes/maryland/tax-general/title-10/subtitle-7/section-10-716/)
- [Form 2441 Instructions - Credit Limit Worksheet](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i2441)

issues.title: NJ: Remove taxable_social_security from subtractions (double exclusion bug)
issues.body:
## Summary

PE incorrectly subtracts taxable Social Security from NJ income, but SS is already excluded from NJ gross income sources. This creates a double exclusion, resulting in significantly underreported NJ tax.

## Root Cause

The bug is in `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/nj/tax/income/subtractions.yaml`:

```yaml
values:
  2021-01-01:
    - taxable_social_security  # BUG: SS already excluded from gross_income_sources
```

The problem:
1. `gross_income_sources.yaml` correctly **excludes** SS from income (SS is not in the list)
2. `subtractions.yaml` incorrectly **subtracts** taxable SS again

This double-counts the SS exclusion.

## Legal Basis

Per NJ tax law and NJ-1040 form:

1. **NJ 54A:5-1** defines gross income as specific categories (wages, interest, dividends, pensions, etc.) - **SS is NOT in this list**
2. **NJ 54A:6-2** explicitly **excludes** federal Social Security from gross income
3. **NJ-1040 Lines 15-26** list income sources - **SS is never entered**

Social Security is simply omitted from NJ income by statute. It's not a "subtraction" - it's excluded by the definition of gross income itself.

## Example

Test case: Single, age 75, $37,274 wages, $27,262 gross SS ($18,869 taxable at federal level)

| Source | NJ Gross Income | SS Subtracted | Taxable Income | Tax |
|--------|-----------------|---------------|----------------|-----|
| TaxAct | $37,274 | $0 | $35,274 | **$552** |
| PE | $37,274 | $18,869 | $16,405 | **$230** |

PE underreports tax by $322 (42% error).

## Fix

Remove `taxable_social_security` from `subtractions.yaml`:

```yaml
# policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/nj/tax/income/subtractions.yaml
values:
  2021-01-01: []  # SS already excluded from gross_income_sources
```

## Files to Modify

- `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/nj/tax/income/subtractions.yaml`

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: NJ single elderly with wages and SS - no double SS exclusion
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 75
        employment_income: 37274.29
        social_security_retirement: 27261.72
        is_tax_unit_head: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1]
        state_fips: 34
  output:
    nj_income_tax: 552  # TaxAct correct value
```

## References

- [NJ 54A:5-1 - Gross income defined](https://law.justia.com/codes/new-jersey/title-54a/section-54a-5-1/)
- [NJ 54A:6-2 - Exclusion of Social Security](https://law.justia.com/codes/new-jersey/title-54a/section-54a-6-2/)
- [NJ-1040 Form](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/current/1040.pdf)
- TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/666

The Iowa Child and Dependent Care Credit (CDCC) incorrectly uses `ia_net_income` for the percentage lookup, but the Iowa form instructions specify using `ia_taxable_income` (IA 1040, Line 4).

## Root Cause

The IA Child Credits form (supporting details for IA 1040 Line 24) states:
- **Line 2**: "Enter **IA 1040, line 4**" (which is Iowa taxable income)

But the code at `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ia/tax/income/credits/ia_cdcc.py:21` uses:

```python
netinc = add(tax_unit, period, ["ia_net_income"])  # BUG
```

| Income for % lookup | **$0** (taxable) | **$20,000** (net) |

issues.title: OK Sales Tax Relief Credit: Capital gains should be netted before applying positive-only rule
issues.body:
## Summary

The Oklahoma Sales Tax Relief Credit (`ok_stc`) incorrectly denies eligible taxpayers when they have both short-term capital losses and long-term capital gains. The `ok_gross_income` variable treats STCG and LTCG separately instead of netting them first.

## Root Cause

**File**: `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ok/tax/income/credits/ok_gross_income.py`

Lines 20-22:
```python
for source in p.credits.gross_income_sources:
    # gross income includes only positive amounts (i.e., no losses)
    income += max_(0, add(tax_unit, period, [source]))
```

This applies `max_(0, ...)` to each income source separately:
- STCG: max(0, -$12,311) = **$0**
- LTCG: max(0, $18,713) = **$18,713**
- Total CG contribution: **$18,713**

Per Form 538-S Line 11 ("Enter gross (positive) income from... gains from the sale or exchange of property"), capital gains should be **netted first**:
- Net CG = -$12,311 + $18,713 = $6,402
- max(0, $6,402) = **$6,402**

## Impact

For a taxpayer with:
- Age 70 (qualifies for $50,000 income limit)
- STCG: -$12,311, LTCG: $18,713
- Dividends: $6,096, Interest: $1,551, Social Security: $24,517

| Calculation | PE (Wrong) | TaxAct (Correct) |
|-------------|------------|------------------|
| Capital Gains | $18,713 | $6,402 |
| **Total Gross Income** | **$50,877** | **$38,565** |
| Income Limit (age 65+) | $50,000 | $50,000 |
| **Eligible?** | **NO** | **YES** |
| Sales Tax Credit | $0 | $80 |

## Suggested Fix

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    p = parameters(period).gov.states.ok.tax.income
    income = 0

    # Handle capital gains specially - net them first per Form 538-S
    stcg = add(tax_unit, period, ["short_term_capital_gains"])
    ltcg = add(tax_unit, period, ["long_term_capital_gains"])
    net_capital_gains = stcg + ltcg
    income += max_(0, net_capital_gains)

    # Handle other income sources normally
    capital_gain_sources = {"short_term_capital_gains", "long_term_capital_gains"}
    for source in p.credits.gross_income_sources:
        if source not in capital_gain_sources:
            income += max_(0, add(tax_unit, period, [source]))

    return income
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: OK Sales Tax Relief Credit with capital loss offset
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 70
        short_term_capital_gains: -6155.5
        long_term_capital_gains: 9356.39
        qualified_dividend_income: 3048.11
        taxable_interest_income: 775.49
        social_security_retirement: 12258.43
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 58
        short_term_capital_gains: -6155.5
        long_term_capital_gains: 9356.39
        qualified_dividend_income: 3048.11
        taxable_interest_income: 775.49
        social_security_retirement: 12258.43
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 40
  output:
    ok_stc: 80
```

## References

- [Form 538-S Instructions](https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/tax/documents/forms/individuals/current/511-Pkt.pdf)

issues.title: MT federal income tax deduction should be eliminated for 2024+
issues.body:
## Summary

Montana eliminated the federal income tax deduction starting with tax year 2024 under Senate Bill 399. PE still applies this deduction, causing a $10,000 overstatement of MT itemized deductions for joint filers.

## Root Cause

PE's `mt_federal_income_tax_deduction_unit` adds up to $10,000 (joint) / $5,000 (other) to MT itemized deductions. This deduction was **eliminated** in 2024 when MT simplified its tax system to use federal taxable income as the starting point.

From the [2024 MT Form 2 Instructions](https://taxsim.nber.org/historical_state_tax_forms/MT/2024/Form_2_2024_Instrux.pdf):

> "Line 2 – Federal standard deduction or **adjusted federal itemized deductions**. You must use the **same type of deduction taken on your federal return** to determine Montana taxable income."

The instructions also confirm:
> "Discontinued Worksheets and Schedules... **●Itemized Deductions Schedule**"

## Test Case (Issue #592)

- Filing: Joint, 2024, MT
- Income: $30,000 wages + $141,201 interest
- Mortgage Interest: $60,400

| Component | TaxAct (Correct) | PE (Bug) |
|-----------|------------------|----------|
| Mortgage Interest | $60,400 | $60,400 |
| MT Federal Tax Deduction | $0 | $10,000 |
| **Total MT Itemized** | **$60,400** | **$70,400** |

## Files to Fix

1. **Create new parameter file:**
   `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/mt/tax/income/deductions/itemized/federal_income_tax/applies.yaml`

```yaml
description: Montana allows a deduction for federal income taxes paid as an itemized deduction, if this is true.
metadata:
  label: Montana federal income tax deduction applies
  period: year
  unit: bool
  reference:
    - title: Montana Tax Reform Update (2024)
      href: https://mtrevenue.gov/montana-tax-simplification-resource-hub/
    - title: Montana State Senate Bill 399 (2021)
      href: https://archive.legmt.gov/bills/2021/sesslaws/ch0503.pdf
    - title: 2024 Montana Form 2 Instructions (Line 2)

```

2. **Update variable:**
   `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/mt/tax/income/deductions/itemized/federal_tax/mt_federal_income_tax_deduction_unit.py`

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    p = parameters(period).gov.states.mt.tax.income.deductions.itemized.federal_income_tax
    
    # Federal income tax deduction eliminated in 2024 under SB 399
    if not p.applies:
        return 0
    
    filing_status = tax_unit("filing_status", period)
    federal_income_tax_limit = p.cap[filing_status]
    federal_income_tax = tax_unit("income_tax_before_refundable_credits", period)
    return min_(federal_income_tax, federal_income_tax_limit)
```

issues.title: MA income tax doesn't allow short-term capital losses to offset long-term capital gains
issues.body:
## Summary

Massachusetts income tax calculation doesn't allow short-term capital losses to offset long-term capital gains in Part C. This results in $398,145 tax when there should be $0 tax.

## Root Cause

In `ma_part_c_gross_income.py`, the formula uses gross long-term capital gains without applying short-term losses:

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    return max_(0, add(tax_unit, period, ["long_term_capital_gains"]))
```

Per MA Schedule B line 22, short-term capital losses should be applied against long-term capital gains before taxation. The TaxAct Form shows:
- Line 15 (STCG losses): -$9,670,468
- Line 22 (Short-term losses applied against long-term gains): -$9,670,468
- Line 23 (LTCG to apply against): $4,900,961
- Result: $0 taxable LTCG (with carryover loss of -$4,769,507)

## Test Case

- Filing: MA joint 2024
- Short-term capital gains: -$9,670,468 (loss)
- Long-term capital gains: +$4,900,962 (gain)
- No other income

**Expected (per TaxAct Form 1 & Schedule B):**
- MA Part C taxable income: $0 (STCG losses offset LTCG)
- MA Tax: $0

**Actual (PE):**
- MA Part C taxable income: $4,892,162 (gross LTCG minus exemption)
- MA Tax: $398,145

## Files to Fix

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ma/tax/income/gross_income/ma_part_c_gross_income.py`

## Suggested Fix

Apply short-term capital losses against long-term capital gains:

```python
def formula(tax_unit, period, parameters):
    ltcg = add(tax_unit, period, ["long_term_capital_gains"])
    stcg = add(tax_unit, period, ["short_term_capital_gains"])
    # STCG losses offset LTCG per MA Schedule B line 22
    stcg_losses = min_(0, stcg)
    return max_(0, ltcg + stcg_losses)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: MA joint with STCG losses offsetting LTCG should have zero Part C tax
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -4835234
        long_term_capital_gains: 2450480.75
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -4835234
        long_term_capital_gains: 2450480.75
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 25
  output:
    ma_part_c_taxable_income: 0
    ma_income_tax: 0
```

## References

- [MA Schedule B Instructions](https://www.mass.gov/doc/2024-schedule-b-interest-dividends-and-certain-capital-gains-and-losses/download) - Line 22: Short-term losses applied against long-term gains
- [MA General Laws Chapter 62 Section 2](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/mass-general-laws-c62-ss-2) - Part C income definition
- Related TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/615

issues.title: MT income tax incorrectly creates phantom income when subtracting capital losses
issues.body:
## Summary

Montana income tax calculation creates phantom taxable income when taxpayers have long-term capital losses. This results in $90,608 tax when there should be $0 tax.

## Root Cause

In `mt_regular_income_tax_joint.py` and `mt_regular_income_tax_indiv.py`, lines 18-20:

```python
if p.capital_gains.in_effect:
    capital_gains = add(tax_unit, period, ["long_term_capital_gains"])
    taxable_income = max_(taxable_income - capital_gains, 0)
```

When `long_term_capital_gains` is **negative** (a loss), subtracting a negative becomes addition:
- `taxable_income` = $0
- `capital_gains` = -$3,141,394 (loss)
- `taxable_income - capital_gains` = $0 - (-$3,141,394) = **$3,141,394** (phantom income!)

This phantom income gets taxed at regular rates.

## Test Case

- Filing: MT joint 2024
- Interest income: $23.71
- Short-term capital gains: -$3,063,628 (loss)
- Long-term capital gains: -$3,141,394 (loss)

**Expected (per TaxAct Form 2):**
- Federal AGI: -$2,976 (interest minus $3,000 capital loss limit)
- MT taxable income: $0
- MT Tax: $0

**Actual (PE):**
- MT Tax: $90,608 (from phantom $3.14M "ordinary income")

## Files to Fix

1. `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/mt/tax/income/tax_calculation/mt_regular_income_tax_joint.py`
2. `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/mt/tax/income/tax_calculation/mt_regular_income_tax_indiv.py`

## Suggested Fix

Only subtract capital gains when they're positive (gains, not losses):

```python
if p.capital_gains.in_effect:
    capital_gains = add(tax_unit, period, ["long_term_capital_gains"])
    capital_gains = max_(capital_gains, 0)  # Don't subtract losses
    taxable_income = max_(taxable_income - capital_gains, 0)
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: MT joint with only capital losses should have zero tax
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -1531814.15
        long_term_capital_gains: -1570696.9
        taxable_interest_income: 11.85
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -1531814.15
        long_term_capital_gains: -1570696.9
        taxable_interest_income: 11.85
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 30
  output:
    mt_income_tax: 0  # From TaxAct - no income means no tax
```

## References

- [Montana Form 2 Instructions](https://mtrevenue.gov/taxes/individual-income-tax/) - Capital gains taxed separately since 2024
- Related TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/616

issues.title: MS income tax incorrectly allows unlimited capital losses to offset income
issues.body:
## Summary

Mississippi income tax calculation allows unlimited capital losses to offset ordinary income, instead of using the federal $3,000 capital loss limit. This results in $0 tax when there should be ~$17,136 tax.

## Root Cause

`policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/ms/tax/income/income_sources.yaml` includes `capital_gains` which is the raw sum of `short_term_capital_gains + long_term_capital_gains` without applying the federal capital loss limitation.

MS Form 80-105 Line 40 ("Capital gain (loss)") flows from federal Schedule D, which already has the $3,000 loss limit applied. PE should use the loss-limited amount.

## Test Case

- Filing: MS joint 2024
- Interest income: $404,179
- Short-term capital gains: -$9,670,468
- Long-term capital gains: +$4,900,962
- Net capital loss: -$4,769,506 (limited to -$3,000 federally)

**Expected (per TaxAct Form 80-105):**
- MS AGI per spouse: ~$200,589
- MS Tax: $17,136

**Actual (PE):**
- MS AGI: $0 (because unlimited -$4.77M loss offsets $404K interest)
- MS Tax: $0

## Files to Fix

1. Create new person-level variable `loss_limited_capital_gains` that allocates `loss_limited_net_capital_gains` (TaxUnit) proportionally to persons
2. Update `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/ms/tax/income/income_sources.yaml` to use `loss_limited_capital_gains` instead of `capital_gains`

## Suggested Implementation

```python
# New file: policyengine_us/variables/household/income/person/capital_gains/loss_limited_capital_gains.py
from policyengine_us.model_api import *

class loss_limited_capital_gains(Variable):
    value_type = float
    entity = Person
    label = "Loss-limited capital gains (person's share)"
    unit = USD
    definition_period = YEAR

    def formula(person, period, parameters):
        # Get person's raw capital gains
        person_capital_gains = person("capital_gains", period)
        
        # Get tax unit totals
        tax_unit_capital_gains = person.tax_unit.sum(person_capital_gains)
        tax_unit_loss_limited = person.tax_unit("loss_limited_net_capital_gains", period)
        
        # If no capital gains, return 0
        # If gains (positive), return person's share unchanged
        # If losses, allocate the loss-limited amount proportionally
        is_loss = tax_unit_capital_gains < 0
        
        # For losses: allocate loss_limited amount proportionally
        proportion = where(
            tax_unit_capital_gains != 0,
            person_capital_gains / tax_unit_capital_gains,
            0
        )
        
        return where(
            is_loss,
            tax_unit_loss_limited * proportion,
            person_capital_gains
        )
```

Then update `income_sources.yaml`:
```yaml
# Change capital_gains to loss_limited_capital_gains
- loss_limited_capital_gains  # Was: capital_gains
```

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: MS joint with capital losses should use federal $3,000 limit
  absolute_error_margin: 100
  period: 2024
  input:
    people:
      person1:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -4835234
        long_term_capital_gains: 2450480.75
        taxable_interest_income: 202089.485
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      person2:
        age: 40
        short_term_capital_gains: -4835234
        long_term_capital_gains: 2450480.75
        taxable_interest_income: 202089.485
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    spm_units:
      spm_unit:
        members: [person1, person2]
    households:
      household:
        members: [person1, person2]
        state_fips: 28
  output:
    ms_income_tax: 17136  # From TaxAct Form 80-105
```

## References

- [MS Form 80-105 Instructions](https://www.dor.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Forms/Individual/80100241.pdf) - Line 40: "Capital gain (loss) (attach Federal Schedule D)"
- [Federal Schedule D](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sd.pdf) - Line 21 limits capital losses to $3,000
- Related TAXSIM issue: https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/617

## Note

This fix may affect other states that use `capital_gains` in their income sources. Review needed for: any state that starts from federal AGI or uses federal Schedule D amounts should use `loss_limited_capital_gains` instead of `capital_gains`.

## Related Issues

- PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim#617: MS 2024 joint 4900Kltcg -9670Kstcg

issues.title: Microsimulation runner doesn't split investment income between spouses
issues.body:
## Summary

The `PolicyEngineRunner` (Microsimulation-based) allocates all investment income to the primary taxpayer, while the situation-based `input_mapper` correctly splits it 50/50 between spouses for married filing jointly. This causes incorrect state tax calculations for states with combined separate filing options (like Delaware and DC).

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_taxsim/runners/policyengine_runner.py`, the `_get_taxsim_to_pe_variable_mapping()` method (lines 175-286) doesn't implement the 50/50 splitting logic that exists in `input_mapper.py` (lines 27-35, 97-122).

**input_mapper.py** correctly splits these income types:
```python
income_types_to_split = {
    "taxable_interest_income",
    "qualified_dividend_income",
    "long_term_capital_gains",
    "partnership_s_corp_income",
    "taxable_private_pension_income",
    "short_term_capital_gains",
    "social_security_retirement",
}
```

**policyengine_runner.py** assigns all income to primary when no spouse pair variable exists (e.g., `intrec` has no `sintrec`):
```python
variable_mapping[pe_var] = {
    "primary": taxsim_var,
    "spouse": 0.0,  # Bug: should be 50% of total
    "dependent": 0.0,
    "default": 0.0,
}
```

## Impact

For issue #630 (DE joint, $62,857 wages, $2,737 interest, $6,298 LTCG):

| Allocation | Spouse AGI | DE Filing | Tax |
|------------|-----------|-----------|-----|
| 50/50 (correct) | $4,946 | Separate | **$2,914.05** |
| All-to-primary (bug) | $0 | Joint | **$3,026.03** |

The $112 discrepancy occurs because Delaware's `de_files_separately` optimization only benefits when the spouse has income.

## Suggested Fix

Update `_get_taxsim_to_pe_variable_mapping()` to split investment income 50/50 for married filing jointly, matching the logic in `input_mapper.py`:

```python
# Add income types that should be split between spouses
income_types_to_split = {
    "taxable_interest_income",
    "qualified_dividend_income", 
    "long_term_capital_gains",
    "partnership_s_corp_income",
    "taxable_private_pension_income",
    "short_term_capital_gains",
    "social_security_retirement",
}

# In the mapping logic, for income types to split:
if pe_var in income_types_to_split:
    variable_mapping[pe_var] = {
        "primary": lambda row, v=taxsim_var: float(row.get(v, 0)) / 2,
        "spouse": lambda row, v=taxsim_var: float(row.get(v, 0)) / 2,
        "dependent": 0.0,
        "default": 0.0,
    }
```

## Files to Modify

- `policyengine_taxsim/runners/policyengine_runner.py` - `_get_taxsim_to_pe_variable_mapping()` method

## Related Issues

- #630 (DE joint discrepancy - this is the root cause)

issues.title: MS separate/combined filing splits exemptions 50/50 instead of optimal allocation
issues.body:
## Summary

Mississippi's `ms_total_exemptions_indiv` splits exemptions 50/50 between spouses for separate/combined filing, but MS law allows married couples to **optimally allocate** exemptions to minimize total tax. This can result in significant tax overstatement.

## Example

**Test case from TAXSIM issue #657:**
- Joint/Combined filing, both spouses age 75
- Person 1: wages $12,697 + interest $13,148 = AGI $25,845
- Person 2: interest $13,148 = AGI $13,148
- Total exemptions: $15,000 ($12,000 filing status + $3,000 aged)

**2024 MS Tax Rates:**
- $0-$10,000: 0%
- Over $10,000: 4.7%

**TaxAct (optimal exemption allocation):**
- Taxpayer: $25,843 - $4,600 ded - $11,549 exemp = $9,694 taxable → **$0 tax**
- Spouse: $13,146 - $0 ded - $3,451 exemp = $9,695 taxable → **$0 tax**
- **Total: $0** (both under $10K threshold)

**PolicyEngine (50/50 exemption split for separate filing):**
- Person 1: $25,845 - $2,300 - $7,500 = $16,045 taxable → $284.10 tax
- Person 2: $13,148 - $2,300 - $7,500 = $3,348 taxable → $0 tax
- **Total: $284.10**

**PolicyEngine (joint filing - currently chosen as "lower"):**
- Person 1: $25,845 - $4,600 - $15,000 = $6,245 taxable → $0 tax
- Person 2: $13,148 - $0 - $0 = $13,148 taxable → $147.97 tax
- **Total: $147.97**

PE chooses joint ($147.97) over separate ($284.10), but optimal separate allocation gives $0.

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ms/tax/income/exemptions/ms_total_exemptions_indiv.py`, lines 14-17:

```python
def formula(person, period, parameters):
    total_exemptions = person.tax_unit("ms_total_exemptions", period)
    is_head_or_spouse = person("is_tax_unit_head_or_spouse", period)
    halved_exemptions = total_exemptions / 2  # <-- Always 50/50
    return is_head_or_spouse * halved_exemptions
```

## Suggested Fix

Implement optimal exemption allocation for MS combined/separate filing. This requires:

1. For each possible exemption split (taxpayer gets X, spouse gets Y where X + Y = total):
   - Calculate each spouse's taxable income
   - Calculate each spouse's tax
   - Sum total tax

2. Choose the allocation that minimizes total tax

This is a constrained optimization problem. A simple approach would be to allocate exemptions to equalize taxable incomes (keeping both under the $10K threshold when possible).

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: ms_optimal_exemption_allocation_elderly_couple
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      head:
        age: 75
        employment_income: 12696.518
        taxable_interest_income: 13148.1955
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      spouse:
        age: 75
        employment_income: 0
        taxable_interest_income: 13148.1955
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [head, spouse]
    households:
      household:
        members: [head, spouse]
        state_fips: 28
  output:
    ms_income_tax: 0  # TaxAct optimal allocation achieves $0 tax
```

## References
- [MS Form 80-105 Instructions](https://www.dor.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Forms/Individual/80100241.pdf)
- [TAXSIM Issue #657](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/657)
- TaxAct Form 80-105 showing optimal allocation achieving $0 tax

issues.title: NJ Other Retirement Income Exclusion uses wrong income base (only age-eligible person's income)
issues.body:
## Summary

The `nj_other_retirement_income_exclusion` variable incorrectly calculates the maximum exclusion based only on the **age-eligible person's income** rather than the **total tax unit income**.

This results in the exclusion being half of what it should be for joint filers where only one spouse is age-eligible.

## Example

**Test case from TAXSIM issue #663:**
- Joint filers
- Person 1: age 75, interest income $65,158
- Person 2: age 40, interest income $65,158
- Total income: $130,317 (triggers 25% exclusion fraction)

**TaxAct (correct):**
- Maximum exclusion = 0.25 × $130,317 = **$32,579**
- NJ Gross Income = $97,738
- NJ Tax = **$2,459**

**PolicyEngine (incorrect):**
- Maximum exclusion = 0.25 × $65,158 = **$16,290** (only uses age-eligible person's income)
- NJ AGI = $114,027
- NJ Tax = ~$3,360

## Root Cause

In `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/nj/tax/income/exclusions/nj_other_retirement_income_exclusion.py`, lines 36-37:

```python
total_income_person = age_eligible * person("nj_total_income", period)
total_income = tax_unit.sum(total_income_person)
```

This filters to only include income from age-eligible persons (age >= 62). However, per NJ tax rules:
1. The exclusion **eligibility** is based on having at least one age-eligible person (correctly implemented)
2. The exclusion **amount** should be calculated from total tax unit income (incorrectly implemented)

## Fix

Change lines 36-37 to:
```python
total_income = add(tax_unit, period, ["nj_total_income"])
```

This aligns with how `nj_retirement_exclusion_fraction` already uses total tax unit income to determine the exclusion percentage.

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: nj_other_retirement_exclusion_joint_one_elderly
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 5
  input:
    people:
      head:
        age: 75
        taxable_interest_income: 65158
        is_tax_unit_head: true
      spouse:
        age: 40
        taxable_interest_income: 65158
        is_tax_unit_spouse: true
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [head, spouse]
    households:
      household:
        members: [head, spouse]
        state_fips: 34
  output:
    nj_other_retirement_income_exclusion: 32579
    nj_income_tax: 2459
```

## References
- [NJ-1040 Instructions Line 28b](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/current/1040i.pdf#page=21)
- [TAXSIM Issue #663](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/663)
- TaxAct form showing correct $32,579 exclusion

issues.title: VA Spouse Tax Adjustment uses incorrectly prorated VAGI
issues.body:
## Summary

The Virginia Spouse Tax Adjustment (`va_spouse_tax_adjustment`) incorrectly calculates eligibility because `va_agi_person` prorates the combined VA AGI by Federal AGI share, instead of calculating separate VAGI for each spouse with deductions applied to the correct person.

## Test Case (from policyengine-taxsim #664)

- **Head**: Age 75, wages $11,752.73
- **Spouse**: Age 40, wages $55,728.48
- **Filing Status**: Joint
- **Year**: 2024
- **State**: VA

### Expected (per VA Form 760 Worksheet, Page 12):

**Step 1 - Separate VAGI calculation:**
- Head FAGI: $11,752.73
- Head age deduction: $12,000 (age 75 qualifies)
- Head separate VAGI: $11,752.73 - $12,000 = **-$247.27**
- Spouse FAGI: $55,728.48
- Spouse age deduction: $0
- Spouse separate VAGI: $55,728.48 - $0 = **$55,728.48**

**Step 2 - STA Worksheet Line 3 (VAGI less exemptions):**
- Head: max(-$247.27 - $1,730, 0) = **$0**
- Spouse: $55,728.48 - $930 = **$54,798.48**

**Eligibility check:** "If either amount is 0 or less, stop here; you do not qualify for this credit"
- Head's Line 3 = $0 → **NOT ELIGIBLE**
- **Correct Spouse Tax Adjustment: $0**

**Correct VA Tax:**
- Tax before credits: $1,802.22
- VA Rebate: -$400.00
- Spouse Tax Adjustment: **$0**
- **Correct VA Tax: $1,402.22**

### PolicyEngine Result:

**PE's va_agi_person (prorated):**
- Head: $55,481.20 × 17.42% = $9,662.77
- Spouse: $55,481.20 × 82.58% = $45,818.43

**PE's va_agi_less_exemptions_person:**
- Head: $9,662.77 - $930 - $800 = $7,932.77
- Spouse: $45,818.43 - $930 - $0 = $44,888.43

**PE's eligibility:** Both > 0 → eligible (WRONG)
- **PE Spouse Tax Adjustment: $189.50** (WRONG)
- **PE VA Tax: $1,212.72** (WRONG - $189.50 too low)

## Root Cause

**File:** `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/va/tax/income/va_agi_person.py`

```python
def formula(person, period, parameters):
    total_agi = person.tax_unit("va_agi", period)  # Combined VA AGI
    person_agi = person("adjusted_gross_income_person", period)
    total_federal_agi = person.tax_unit.sum(person_agi)
    
    prorate = np.zeros_like(total_agi)
    mask = total_federal_agi > 0
    prorate[mask] = person_agi[mask] / total_federal_agi[mask]
    return total_agi * prorate  # WRONG: prorates combined VA AGI
```

The problem: `va_agi` already has the $12,000 age deduction subtracted. When this is prorated by Federal AGI share, the age deduction gets spread across both spouses (17.42% to head, 82.58% to spouse) instead of applying only to the head.

## Fix Required

`va_agi_person` should calculate each person's separate VAGI by:
1. Starting with each person's Federal AGI
2. Adding person-specific VA additions
3. Subtracting person-specific VA subtractions (age deduction, etc.)

This matches the VA worksheet on Page 12 of the Form 760 instructions, which explicitly shows how to calculate "Separate Virginia Adjusted Gross Income" for each spouse.

## Files to Modify

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/va/tax/income/va_agi_person.py` - Fix proration logic
- May need to create person-level VA subtraction variables

## Integration Test

```yaml
- name: VA Spouse Tax Adjustment - elderly head with low income
  period: 2024
  absolute_error_margin: 1
  input:
    people:
      head:
        age: 75
        employment_income: 11752.73
      spouse:
        age: 40
        employment_income: 55728.48
    tax_units:
      tax_unit:
        members: [head, spouse]
    households:
      household:
        members: [head, spouse]
        state_code: VA
  output:
    va_spouse_tax_adjustment: 0  # Head's VAGI less exemptions <= 0, not eligible
    va_income_tax: 1402.22  # $1,802.22 - $400 rebate - $0 STA
```

## Sources

- [VA Form 760 Instructions 2024 - Page 12 (Spouse Tax Adjustment Worksheet)](https://www.tax.virginia.gov/sites/default/files/vatax-pdf/2024-760-instructions.pdf)
- [policyengine-taxsim Issue #664](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/664)

issues.title: AZ Property Tax Credit uses wrong income definition (includes aged exemption)
issues.body:
## Summary

The Arizona property tax credit (`az_property_tax_credit`) uses `az_agi` in its income calculation, which incorrectly includes the $2,100 aged exemption deduction. Per ARS 43-1072 and Arizona Admin Code R15-2C-502, the "household income" for property tax credit purposes should NOT include Arizona exemptions.

## Test Case (from [policyengine-taxsim](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/654) )

- **Age**: 75
- **Wages**: $3,715.56
- **Interest**: $50.52
- **Rent Paid**: $928.89/month ($11,146.68/year)
- **Filing Status**: Single
- **Year**: 2024

### Expected (per TaxAct/Form 140PTC):
- Household Income: $3,766.08 (Federal AGI)
- Threshold (living alone): $3,751
- $3,766.08 > $3,751 → **NOT ELIGIBLE** for property tax credit
- Property Tax Credit: **$0**
- Increased Excise Tax Credit: **$25**
- Total AZ refund: **$25**

### PolicyEngine Result:
- Uses `az_agi` = $1,666.08 ($3,766.08 - $2,100 aged exemption)
- $1,666.08 < $3,751 → incorrectly shows eligible
- Property Tax Credit: **$502** (incorrect)
- Total AZ refund: **$527** (incorrect)

## Root Cause

**File**: `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/az/tax/income/credits/property_tax/income_sources.yaml`

```yaml
values:
  2021-01-01:
    - capital_gains_excluded_from_taxable_income
    - tax_exempt_interest_income
    - public_pension_income
    - az_agi   # <-- PROBLEM: includes aged/blind exemptions
```

The `az_agi` variable (in `az_agi.py`) subtracts `az_exemptions` (which includes `az_aged_exemption` of $2,100). But the Form 140PTC "household income" definition per ARS 43-1072(H)(6) and Admin Code R15-2C-502 does NOT subtract these exemptions.

## Legal References

**ARS 43-1072(H)(6)(a)**:
> "Adjusted gross income" as defined by the department.

**Arizona Admin Code R15-2C-502(A)(1)**:
> "Adjusted gross income" means the sum of all income not specifically excluded in A.R.S. § 43-1072 whether or not subject to Arizona income tax, except those items that A.R.S. § 43-1072 specifically includes in income.

This is a custom definition that is essentially Federal AGI + certain additions - certain exclusions (SS benefits, etc.), but **NOT** minus Arizona exemptions.

## Suggested Fix

**Option 1**: Create a new variable `az_property_tax_credit_household_income` that calculates income per Form 140PTC definition (Federal AGI + additions - exclusions per ARS 43-1072, without AZ exemptions).

**Option 2**: Modify `income_sources.yaml` to use `adjusted_gross_income` (Federal AGI) instead of `az_agi`, plus the specific add-backs required by Form 140PTC.

**Option 3**: Create `az_property_tax_credit_agi` that starts with Federal AGI and only applies the specific adjustments defined in ARS 43-1072(H)(6), not the general AZ exemptions.

## Files to Modify

- `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/az/tax/income/credits/property_tax/income_sources.yaml`
- Possibly create new variable for Form 140PTC household income definition

## Sources

- [ARS 43-1072 - Property Tax Credit](https://www.azleg.gov/viewdocument/?docName=https://www.azleg.gov/ars/43/01072.htm)
- [Arizona Admin Code R15-2C-502](https://apps.azsos.gov/public_services/Title_15/15-02.pdf)
- [2024 Form 140PTC Instructions](https://azdor.gov/forms/individual/property-tax-refund-credit-claim)
- [policyengine-taxsim Issue #654](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/policyengine-taxsim/issues/654)

prs.title: feat: Allow multiple instances of the dev server to run simultaneously
prs.body:
## Summary

- Adds automatic port discovery for dev servers, allowing multiple instances to run simultaneously
- Creates a launcher script (`scripts/dev-server.mjs`) that finds available ports starting from 3000
- Ports are automatically passed to Vite via environment variables
- Each instance gets its own consecutive port pair (e.g., 3000/3001, 3002/3003)

## How it works

When running `make dev`:
1. The launcher script checks ports starting from 3000
2. It detects occupied ports by attempting TCP connections on both IPv4 and IPv6
3. Once two consecutive available ports are found, it passes them to the Vite dev servers
4. The vite config reads `WEBSITE_PORT` and `CALCULATOR_PORT` and configures servers accordingly
5. Cross-app URLs are derived from these ports automatically

## Usage

```bash
# Terminal 1
make dev
# → "Dev servers: Website :3000, Calculator :3001"

# Terminal 2 (while first is running)
make dev
# → "Dev servers: Website :3002, Calculator :3003"
```

## Test plan

- [x] Run `make dev` in one terminal - verify website on :3000, calculator on :3001
- [x] Run `make dev` in second terminal - verify it auto-discovers :3002/:3003
